1:
Henry begins with the second look. The prophet is brought back over ground already surveyed, which Henry takes for a lesson, since the things of God bear looking over again and every review turns up something new. He is led a third time to the eastern gate and finds it shut, which implies the others stood open, the difference perpetuating the memory of the glory that had entered there. Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter out in three parts: the prince's place at the temple service, the admission of foreigners with the appointment of Levites and priests, and the duties of the priestly office.

Which court the gate belongs to is not agreed. Gill has the prophet brought from the altar to the holy place, called the outward sanctuary to distinguish it from the holy of holies, and takes the gate for one of the inner court, as Henry does. Ellicott renders the phrase as the outer gate of the sanctuary, bringing the prophet out of the inner court where the altar stood to the eastern gate of the outer. Clarke adds that the gate opened only on sabbaths and new moons, and records that the verse has been pressed into an argument about the mother of Jesus, allows it is as much to the purpose as others offered for that conclusion, and calls the point precarious, one no man should lay stress on.

Who the prince is divides them more sharply. Gill runs through the candidates and rejects two: not the high priest, though one rabbi says so and he might have had a seat as an earlier priest had, and not the civil ruler, though the Jews allow only kings of David's house might sit in the sanctuary. He settles with two other Jewish commentators on the Messiah. Ellicott agrees the rabbis were right and the person must be the David named earlier in the book, drawing from it that this is decisive for treating the sacrificial worship of these chapters as symbolic. He refuses to narrow the eating: the phrase is the ordinary one for partaking of sacrifices, and confining it to the unbloody offerings will not do, since eating those was a priestly prerogative and this prince, however distinguished, has no priestly function. Wesley keeps the civil sense, that the king might sit before the Lord where others might not, and takes the bread for the offerer's portion.

At the north gate the charge is to observe. Ellicott argues from its being called before the house, in full view of it, that this must be the inner gate, the place appointed for killing sacrifices and so fitting for publishing the priests' ordinances. Henry draws the posture into a maxim, that the more we see of God's glory the lower we lie in our own eyes, and notes that what the prophet must mark especially is the going in and the going out. Clarke makes it a duty of record, to register everything so fully that the most minute information could be given afterwards. Wesley glosses the entering as who may and may not come in, takes the sanctuary for the courts rather than the house, and identifies the guide as Christ in the appearance of a man.

The closing censure turns on a distinction. Ellicott points out that foreigners in Israel were allowed and sometimes required to sacrifice, as the prayer at the first temple's dedication recognised; what is condemned is admitting men uncircumcised in heart as well as flesh, with no real intention of worshipping. Gill takes the strangers spiritually, for the unregenerate, strangers to God, to Christ and to their own hearts. Clarke observes that the fat and the blood never went to common use, one poured out and the other consumed, and reports manuscripts reading their abominations rather than yours, referring the fault to the strangers; Wesley keeps it on the nation.
10:
When the apostasy happened is disputed. Clarke refers the degraded Levites to the schism of the northern kingdom, when the new king drew as many priests as he could into his worship, and holds that on the return these might not serve at the altar though they could be kept as treasurers, guards and porters, the whole passage belonging to the second temple. Ellicott says the opposite: at that crisis these priests stood firm, and it was in the later general decline that many fell into idolatry. He also sharpens the join with what precedes, the first words being better rendered yea, even: not the uncircumcised heathen only are shut out, but the Levites too must bear their guilt. Henry pictures a householder setting up again and taking account of his servants, naming the compliances: priests who bowed in an idol's house or built an altar for a king, and so led a nation into sin, since when priests go astray many follow. Gill turns it into a description of ministers who departed from the principles they professed, mixed the faith with the doctrines of men and made their own reason their guide.

The sentence on them is demotion rather than dismissal. Wesley makes them servants in the lowest work, porters to open and shut and sweep and wait on the priests, confining the sanctuary they keep to the courts. Ellicott finds the precedent in the older law, where a priest with a bodily blemish might serve in humbler offices but not come to the altar. Gill draws a disciplinary parallel, that ministers who had sinned foully were formerly not restored to office on repentance but admitted only to lay communion.

Against them stand the sons of Zadok. Ellicott takes the phrase for a description rather than a genealogy: as the man himself stayed loyal in a rebellion where even the high priest and the king's lifelong friend went over, so any priest who kept faith in an apostasy is called by his name. Gill keeps the descent, through Eleazar in the line of Phinehas, and adds that the name means righteous. Wesley reads the reward as a rule, that God puts marks of honour on those faithful in trying times and employs those who kept to his service when others drew back.

Why the priests may wear no wool is the sharpest split here. Henry takes the reason given in the text, that wool causes sweat: they must dress cool to move readily about work done beside altars that burn constantly, and clean, to signify the purity of mind with which God is to be served; and he recalls that sweat came in with sin and belongs to the curse. Clarke supplies different reasons. Wool contracts dirt and breeds insects where linen breeds none; and beyond that, one is a vegetable and the other an animal substance, on the ancient maxim that whatever is taken from a dead body is unclean in religion. He supports it from elsewhere: Egyptian priests wore linen with shoes of matting, and Muslims will not write their scripture on skin, counting it a defilement. Gill leaves the physical question alone and makes the linen headgear a sign of gravity, subjection to God and purity of doctrine.

The changing of clothes is treated as a new rule. Ellicott observes that wearing the official dress only on duty, putting it on at the inner court and off on leaving, is merely implied in the older books and here expressly commanded, and notes the old word utter simply means outer. Wesley explains the danger guarded against, since by the law common things touching holy things became consecrated and no longer fit for common use. Keil and Delitzsch keep the sequence of the requirements, the linen bonnets and breeches, the prohibition of anything causing sweat, and the laying up of the garments in the holy chambers.
20:
The hair rule is set against foreign practice. Gill and Clarke both name the shaven priests of an Egyptian cult, Clarke adding that the priests of an Eastern religion still shave close every tenth day; Gill names a modern clergy from whom faithful ministers must differ. Ellicott looks at the law: shaving the head was forbidden outright, long hair condemned only by implication, since the older code allowed it in the case of a vow. Wesley supplies the vanity it guards against, naming a prince who prided himself on his hair, and reads the polling as keeping it moderate.

How far the wine is forbidden divides two of them. Wesley ties the prohibition to the duty, so that it holds when they go to trim the lamps, set out the bread or approach the altar, and extends it to strong drink. Gill limits it to excess, holding wine not forbidden to ministers for health's sake if taken in moderation, and treats sobriety as a standing qualification.

On marriage and mourning Ellicott makes the chapter's most consequential observation. The older law drew a broad line between the ordinary priest and the high priest: the one was forbidden only a divorced wife and might marry a widow, the other might marry none but a virgin, and could not mourn even his nearest kin. This prophet does not keep that distinction, and never mentions a high priest at all, but lays down one rule for all, falling between the two older ones. Clarke notices half the same fact, that the bar on marrying a widow had been the high priest's alone.

Gill takes the teaching and judging clauses into his own idiom. The difference between holy and profane is to be taught in no ceremonial or merely moral sense but an evangelical one, between truth and error, between the doctrine that is according to godliness and what is corrupt; and controversies are not to go before a court of the men of the world but be heard in the church, its ministers presiding and standing by their sentence. Wesley keeps it plainer, glossing the assemblies as public congregations.

The defilement rules are read as a tightening. Ellicott observes that they repeat the older law almost exactly, with one addition: on top of the ordinary seven days of cleansing a second seven is required, then a sin offering before the priest resumes. Wesley states the doubling as administration, the other priests appointing the further term. Gill gives a practical reason, that the work not be interrupted nor the man unfitted by grief, and a spiritual one, that there be no fellowship with those dead in sins. Clarke notes that contact with the dead still defiles among another living people, who must bathe to be clean.

The priests' maintenance draws Clarke off the text altogether. Those who profess to model their church order on the Jewish one have all, he says, left this clause out: they will not live on free offerings but must have revenues secured by law. He grants that every minister should live by the altar, but would rather assign each land enough for his keep, or let the state maintain him as it does its other officers, given the dissension the present way of paying parish clergy breeds. Ellicott adds that being told God is their inheritance never excluded their having cities with pasture around them.

Gill closes on a puzzle he cannot solve. The Jewish doctors noticed that the ban on eating what died of itself is addressed to the priests, which seems to imply that Israelites might; unable to account for it, they said Elijah would explain the verse, and until he comes they do not know. Ellicott removes the difficulty: the same law bound every Israelite, who threw such meat to the dogs in the wilderness and afterwards might give or sell it to a foreigner.
